strengths: M4Human addresses a meaningful gap in computer vision and RF sensing: existing radar datasets largely provide sparse skeleton labels, whereas this dataset pairs radar with marker-based motion capture and SMPL-X-style meshes for human mesh reconstruction.

The dataset is substantial in duration and modality coverage: 661K synchronized frames, 999 sequences, 50 actions, 20 subjects, RGB, depth, radar point clouds, and radar tensors. Including dynamic sports and rehabilitation motions is especially valuable compared with predominantly in-place prior datasets.

The evaluation covers random, cross-subject, and cross-action splits, multiple action regimes, four mesh/pose metrics in the world coordinate frame, several radar baselines, camera modalities, multimodal fusion, data-scaling experiments, and downstream action recognition.

The results reveal useful conclusions beyond leaderboard performance. In particular, raw radar tensors generalize better than point clouds on the cross-subject and cross-action settings, while the large degradation on non-in-place motions identifies an important open problem.

RT-Mesh is a sensible, computationally efficient baseline. Its localization-then-cropping design reduces full-volume processing cost and achieves the best reported radar results on most cross-subject and cross-action comparisons at 2.60 GFLOPs and 2.74 ms latency.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and its figures and tables clearly communicate the sensing setup, dataset scope, protocols, and principal empirical findings.
weaknesses: The central claim of high-fidelity ground truth is insufficiently validated. Meshes are not measured directly: 37 marker trajectories are passed through the learned SOMA reconstruction system. The paper provides no marker-to-mesh fitting error, held-out marker error, joint or surface accuracy, failure rate, inter-rater audit, or comparison against an independent reference. Manual visualization cannot establish annotation accuracy quantitatively.

Temporal synchronization is potentially consequential for the fast sports motions emphasized by the paper. Radar and RGB-D are alternately polled at 12 Hz, while synchronization to the 100 Hz Vicon stream uses a manually located trigger followed by nearest-frame matching. No hardware synchronization, clock-drift correction, timestamp-error distribution, or motion-dependent alignment test is reported.

Calibration quality is asserted but not measured. The manuscript gives the PnP procedure but omits reprojection residuals, 3D cross-modal alignment errors, repeatability across recording sessions, and whether calibration was repeated when the apparatus moved. These omissions weaken confidence in world-frame MVE and translation-error results.

The split construction is ambiguous and may permit temporal leakage. The random protocol says that clips are assigned to non-overlapping subsets, but does not define clip boundaries or confirm sequence-level splitting. With densely sampled frames and four-frame temporal inputs, neighboring portions of the same recording could occur in training and testing. Exact split lists and safeguards against overlapping temporal windows are needed.

The dataset is large mainly in correlated frame count but remains limited to 20 subjects, one apparent capture environment, and one radar system. Cross-subject testing uses only four participants and apparently a single split, with no uncertainty or variation across alternative subject/action partitions. Generalization across rooms, clothing, occlusion, sensor placement, distance strata, or radar hardware is not evaluated.

Several broad motivations and claims are not directly supported experimentally. The paper does not test adverse lighting, occlusion, smoke, privacy leakage, or cross-environment robustness; consequently, claims about real-world robustness and privacy-preserving deployment remain largely inherited from radar's presumed properties.

Reproducibility is weak in the supplied manuscript. RT-Mesh losses and detailed architecture are deferred to an unavailable supplementary document, while training hyperparameters, preprocessing, data formats, fusion implementation, action definitions, split identities, storage requirements, and complete latency hardware/protocol are absent. The dataset and code are only promised after publication, preventing present verification.

The claimed raw radar tensor is already FFT-processed and mapped into Cartesian coordinates by a proprietary sensing pipeline, rather than being raw time-domain measurements. The paper should use more precise terminology and document the processing chain, calibration, tensor units, dynamic range, and proprietary dependencies.

Some interpretations are overstated. Three training-set sizes do not establish a scaling law, and the effective-point ratio comparison with mmBody lacks a precise neighborhood definition and controls for different sensors and filtering pipelines. There are also citation inconsistencies, such as labeling mm-Mesh with reference [44] in Table 2 although mmMesh is reference [43].

Overall, the benchmark has clear potential and likely community value, but missing quantitative validation of its synchronization, calibration, and mesh annotations affects the reliability of its core contribution. These are material scientific concerns rather than merely presentation refinements, placing the paper near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The submission targets an important and comparatively underexplored problem: privacy-preserving human mesh reconstruction from mmWave radar. Providing synchronized radar tensors, radar point clouds, RGB-D, and marker-based motion capture could be useful to both RF sensing and computer-vision researchers.

The proposed dataset is substantial in duration and action coverage: 661K frames, approximately 15.3 hours, 999 sequences, 50 actions, and both in-place and free-space motions. The inclusion of rehabilitation and sports actions is a meaningful advance over datasets dominated by simple daily activities.

The evaluation includes random, cross-subject, and cross-action splits, and reports world-coordinate vertex, joint, rotation, and translation errors. Separating translation from articulated-pose error is especially appropriate for free-space motion.

The paper supplies several useful initial benchmarks, including RPC- and tensor-based models, multimodal fusion, training-scale studies, and downstream action recognition. RT-Mesh is a computationally efficient baseline for the tensor representation.
weaknesses: The central claim of high-quality, precisely aligned ground truth is insufficiently validated. Synchronization relies on a manually identified head-swing event, alternating 12 Hz sensor polling on one computer, and nearest-neighbor matching to 100 Hz Vicon data. No temporal-offset or drift measurement is reported. Likewise, calibration uses manually selected correspondences but provides no reprojection, 3D alignment, or repeatability error. These omissions materially affect the reliability of world-coordinate mesh and translation evaluation.

The meshes are estimates produced by SOMA from 37 marker trajectories rather than directly observed ground truth, yet the paper reports no quantitative mesh-fitting accuracy, marker residuals, failure rate, or comparison against an independent measurement. Describing the labels as high-fidelity is therefore plausible but not demonstrated.

The random split is potentially vulnerable to severe temporal leakage. The paper says that clips are randomly assigned to subsets, but does not state that temporally adjacent or overlapping four-frame windows from the same sequence are kept together. Given the high frame rate and essentially one sequence per subject-action pair, this ambiguity undermines the strong S1 results and associated conclusions.

Reproducibility is currently poor. The dataset and code are only promised after publication, while essential RT-Mesh architecture and loss details are deferred to an unprovided supplement. Training schedules, preprocessing details, split identities, random seeds, latency hardware, and uncertainty across runs are also absent.

The evidence does not support several broad claims. A three-point subset experiment without uncertainty or fitted scaling behavior is called a scaling law; edge deployability is inferred from latency without specifying hardware or end-to-end processing; and robustness to illumination and occlusion is motivated but never tested. Data appear to come from one laboratory and sensing configuration, leaving environmental and device generalization unexamined.

The term “raw radar tensor” is misleading: the released tensor is already FFT-processed, intensity-valued, and mapped into Cartesian coordinates by a proprietary sensing pipeline. The paper does not specify signal preprocessing sufficiently to determine what information is retained or whether the representation can be reproduced on another radar.

Cross-modality comparisons do not isolate sensing quality because each modality uses a different architecture and initialization: RGB uses a large-scale pretrained TokenHMR model, while depth and radar use other adapted models. Consequently, conclusions that radar matches or surpasses RGB-D are confounded by model and training differences.

The benchmark has only 20 subjects, restricted height and weight ranges, and no external or cross-environment test. Frame count substantially overstates independent diversity because consecutive 12 Hz samples are strongly correlated. Fixed split results without repeated splits or confidence intervals make generalization claims fragile.

For a dataset intended for public distribution, governance information is inadequate. The manuscript mentions participant notification and masks/caps but does not report an ethics-review process, consent and withdrawal procedures, licensing, or safeguards for still-identifying RGB and body-motion data.

There are also presentation-level problems—numerous grammatical errors, inconsistent method citations in tables, incompletely specified action categories, and exaggerated wording such as “remarkably” for small or inconsistent fusion gains—but these are secondary to the validation, leakage, and reproducibility concerns above.

strengths: M4Human is a substantial and timely dataset contribution. It provides 661K synchronized frames from 999 sequences, 20 subjects, and 50 actions, and is approximately nine times larger than the prior largest radar-HMR dataset reported by the authors.

The combination of RGB, depth, radar point clouds, radar tensors, and marker-based Vicon capture is valuable. Providing both dense radar tensors and sparsified point clouds should enable research on radar representations, cross-modal learning, and privacy-preserving human sensing.

The action set goes meaningfully beyond mostly stationary daily activities: it includes rehabilitation exercises and dynamic, non-in-place sports motions with global trajectories. This breadth exposes challenging tracking and reconstruction conditions that are underrepresented in existing radar datasets.

The benchmark is comprehensive for a dataset paper. It includes random, cross-subject, and cross-action splits; multiple RPC and RT baselines; RGB/depth comparisons; multimodal fusion; data-scaling experiments; efficiency measurements; and downstream action recognition.

The proposed RT-Mesh baseline is sensible and computationally efficient. Its localization-then-crop design avoids processing the entire 3D radar volume, reaching 2.74 ms and 2.60 GFLOPs while obtaining the best or nearly best radar-only MVE across the reported splits.

The experiments provide useful findings beyond leaderboard numbers. In particular, tensor input generalizes better than point clouds on unseen subjects/actions, increasing training diversity consistently improves generalization, and radar fusion improves several RGB/depth results. The paper also reports world-frame errors without root or Procrustes alignment, making global tracking performance visible.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and visually informative. The dataset motivation, sensing setup, protocols, metrics, and principal empirical conclusions are easy to follow.
weaknesses: The claimed high-fidelity ground truth is not quantitatively validated. Mesh labels are inferred from 37 markers using SOMA and subsequently checked visually, but the paper reports no held-out marker error, reconstruction error, calibration residual, synchronization error, inter-annotator verification, or percentage of frames requiring correction. This is the most important technical limitation because label quality is central to the contribution.

Temporal synchronization is relatively coarse and partly manual: radar and RGB-D are alternately polled at 12 Hz, a head gesture is manually located in RGB, and each sensor frame is matched to the nearest 100 Hz Vicon frame. The manuscript does not measure timestamp offsets or drift over long sequences; such errors could be consequential for the fast sports motions emphasized by the paper.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete. The data and code are promised only after publication, while essential RT-Mesh architecture and loss details are deferred to an unavailable supplementary document. Radar preprocessing, training hyperparameters, latency hardware, licensing, and concrete release/access conditions are also insufficiently specified in the manuscript.

The term “raw radar tensor” is potentially misleading: the released representation is described as an FFT-processed Cartesian intensity volume produced by a proprietary Vayyar sensing pipeline, rather than raw ADC/time-domain measurements. The exact preprocessing, resolution, normalization, and proprietary dependencies should be documented so users understand what can be reproduced or transferred to other devices.

The random split needs a more precise leakage analysis. The paper says clips are randomly assigned, but does not define clip construction or confirm that temporally adjacent/overlapping windows from the same original sequence cannot cross subsets. Because models use four consecutive frames, accidental temporal proximity could inflate S1 results.

Several empirical claims are stronger than the evidence. Fusion gains are called “significant” without statistical tests or repeated-run uncertainty, and RPC+RT provides essentially no S2 MVE improvement over RT alone (135.2 versus 135.1 mm). Likewise, the “scaling law” conclusion is based on only three dataset fractions and is better characterized as a monotonic data-scaling trend.

The comparison does not isolate whether gains arise from dataset scale, the higher-resolution Vayyar device, preprocessing quality, or model design. Cross-dataset evaluation or transfer between M4Human and an existing public radar dataset would materially strengthen claims about generalization and broader usefulness.

Population and capture diversity remain limited despite the large frame count: only 20 subjects, one sensor configuration, one indoor capture environment, and restricted height/weight ranges are described. The paper should temper claims of broad-population or real-world generalizability, especially for healthcare applications.

Ethics and privacy reporting is thin for a dataset intended for public release. Consent and masks/caps are mentioned, but there is no discussion of institutional approval, withdrawal procedures, data governance, license, or residual identity information in RGB, depth, body shape, and motion trajectories. This does not negate the contribution but should be addressed before release.

strengths: M4Human is a substantial and potentially valuable dataset contribution: 661K synchronized frames from 999 sequences, with RGB, depth, raw radar tensors, radar point clouds, and MoCap-derived SMPL-X annotations. The benchmark is unusually comprehensive for this emerging area. It evaluates random, cross-subject, and cross-action splits; separates in-place, seated, and non-in-place motions; reports vertex, joint, rotation, and translation errors; and compares RGB, depth, RPC, RT, and multimodal fusion.

The experiments support the practical value of the resource. For example, increasing RT-Mesh training data reduces cross-subject MVE from 161.0 to 135.1 mm and cross-action MVE from 174.9 to 143.1 mm. The large degradation relative to the random split also identifies genuine remaining generalization challenges rather than presenting only favorable results.

RT-Mesh is a sensible first baseline for raw-tensor HMR. Its BEV localization followed by cropped 3D processing is technically motivated by the size of the radar volume and achieves competitive accuracy with low reported cost of 2.60 GFLOPs and 2.74 ms latency.

The supplementary material provides useful implementation, storage, action-definition, and preprocessing details. The LMDB distribution and lossless sparse tensor representation should make a dataset of this size substantially easier to use.

The downstream action-recognition experiment and multimodal-fusion results demonstrate usefulness beyond a single benchmark metric. In particular, RGB+RT substantially improves over RGB alone across all three splits.
weaknesses: The most important technical weakness is the absence of quantitative ground-truth validation. Meshes are reconstructed from 37 markers using SOMA rather than measured directly, while cross-modal synchronization relies on manually locating a trigger gesture and nearest-frame matching between separate 12 Hz and 100 Hz systems. No marker reprojection error, mesh-to-marker residual, calibration error, synchronization error or drift measurement, inter-annotator check, or failed-frame rate is reported. Qualitative overlays in Figures 3 and 9 do not establish the claimed annotation precision.

Claims that RT contains richer information and generalizes better than RPC are confounded by the use of different encoders: RT-Mesh is compared primarily with P4Transformer for RPC. A controlled experiment using matched capacity and processing, or ablations of RT-Mesh's localization, cropping, temporal window, and transformer components, is missing. Fusion gains show complementarity but do not isolate whether RT's apparent advantage comes from the representation or model design.

The claim that radar is comparable to RGB-D should be qualified. The modalities use substantially different pipelines and priors: RGB uses a cropped TokenHMR model whose pose tokenizer is frozen, while depth and radar receive explicit metric-range measurements and are optimized through other architectures. Thus Table 3 is an informative set of baselines, but not a controlled comparison of the intrinsic sensing modalities.

The dataset covers only 20 subjects in one controlled indoor site with one sensor configuration. There are no cross-room, cross-device, multi-person, severe-occlusion, clothing, smoke, or illumination experiments. Consequently, the evidence supports a strong controlled benchmark but not the broader real-world robustness and deployment claims made in the introduction.

The evaluation does not report uncertainty over training runs or subject/action selections. Because adjacent frames are strongly correlated, the nominal frame count overstates the effective number of independent test observations. The exact unit used for S1 assignment should also be clarified to rule out temporally neighboring windows from the same sequence entering different splits.

Several reproducibility and consistency issues need correction. The public benchmark URL is blank; important dataset license/access terms and release contents are not specified; Table 2 cites mmMesh and P4Transformer with incorrect reference numbers; and P4Transformer values differ between the main and supplementary tables, including 90.4 versus 89.5 mm for S1 ALL and 72.7 versus 71.5 mm for S1 P1. These do not negate the contribution but reduce confidence in the current record.

Privacy is presented too categorically. Radar suppresses visual appearance, but reconstructed shape, gait, and activity can still enable identification or sensitive inference. The ethics discussion acknowledges behavioral monitoring but should avoid describing RF sensing as inherently or completely privacy-preserving.

strengths: The dataset addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: privacy-preserving human mesh reconstruction from mmWave radar. Providing synchronized RGB, depth, radar point clouds, radar tensors, and MoCap-derived meshes could be valuable to both vision and RF-sensing communities.

The reported scale is substantial for radar-based HMR: 661K frames, 999 sequences, 20 subjects, and 50 actions. The inclusion of free-space sports and rehabilitation motions is a meaningful improvement over datasets dominated by simple in-place actions.

The evaluation includes random, cross-subject, and cross-action splits; multiple reconstruction metrics computed without root or Procrustes alignment; comparisons across sensing modalities; and downstream action-recognition experiments.

RT-Mesh is a sensible and efficient baseline. Its localization-then-crop design reduces the cost of processing volumetric radar tensors, and the reported results indicate that tensor representations can generalize better than thresholded point clouds.
weaknesses: The central claim of high-fidelity ground truth is insufficiently validated. Meshes are inferred from 37 markers using SOMA rather than directly measured, yet the paper reports no marker reconstruction error, mesh-fitting error, inter-annotator check, failure rate, or quantitative spatial and temporal calibration accuracy. Visual overlays cannot establish annotation fidelity.

Synchronization is comparatively weak for a dataset making precise motion claims: separate computers are aligned using a manually located gesture, followed by nearest-frame matching between 12 Hz sensor data and 100 Hz Vicon. The paper provides no clock-drift analysis, per-sequence timing error, or hardware synchronization. Errors here would directly contaminate evaluation, especially for the fast motions emphasized as a contribution.

The random split is not defined at sufficient granularity. If clips or frames from the same recorded sequence occur in both training and test sets, temporally adjacent near-duplicates can inflate S1 results. The manuscript should state the splitting unit and temporal separation. Subject identity and body shape can likewise be memorized when the same subjects appear across the split.

The scale study does not isolate dataset size. For S2, increasing from 25% to 100% changes the number of training subjects from 4 to 16; for S3 it changes action diversity from 10 to 40 classes. Improvements therefore conflate sample count with substantially broader subject/action coverage. Only one subset appears to be tested, with no repeated sampling, variance, or uncertainty, so calling the result a 'scaling law' is not supported.

Several comparative conclusions are overstated. Radar remains materially worse than depth in most single-modality results, while claims about robustness to illumination, occlusion, smoke, and clothing are not evaluated on M4Human. All data also come from one indoor setup and one radar, so robustness and real-world deployment claims lack direct evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important RT-Mesh specifications such as transformer depth, width, attention configuration, and downsampling factors N1/N2 are omitted. The stated learning-rate schedule multiplies the rate by 0.1 every five epochs during 100-epoch training, which is unusual and insufficiently explained. No run variance or statistical uncertainty is reported.

The released 'raw radar tensor' is already FFT-processed and mapped to a Cartesian intensity volume, not raw ADC radar measurements. This terminology should be qualified, and the proprietary preprocessing performed by the Vayyar system should be documented because it limits reproducibility and portability to other radars.

The RGB comparison has technical ambiguities: camera-coordinate back-projection is described as producing world coordinates without an explicit extrinsic transformation, and the predicted weak-perspective scale is used to modify both crop coordinates and depth in a nonstandard formulation. These details matter because all metrics are evaluated in the world frame.

The benchmark covers only 20 participants, a single room, and essentially one sequence per subject-action pair. This is appreciable for radar collection but limited evidence for the claimed population, environmental, and deployment generalizability.

The manuscript contains consistency and presentation problems, including incorrect citations in Table 2, an absent public benchmark URL, and repeated claims of being 'largest' or 'first' without sufficiently careful qualification. These are secondary to the annotation, synchronization, and evaluation concerns but further reduce confidence.

strengths: M4Human is a substantial and relevant dataset contribution: 661K synchronized frames, 999 sequences, 50 actions, and 20 subjects make it considerably larger and more behaviorally diverse than prior public radar-based HMR datasets, particularly for free-space sports and rehabilitation motions.

The combination of RGB, depth, radar point clouds, FFT-derived radar tensors, global trajectories, and marker-based MoCap-derived SMPL-X annotations is unusually comprehensive. Providing both dense radar tensors and processed point clouds should enable research beyond the specific baseline presented.

The evaluation is broad for a dataset paper. It covers random, cross-subject, and cross-action splits; in-place, seated, and non-in-place motions; four reconstruction metrics; multiple radar baselines; RGB/depth comparisons; multimodal fusion; dataset-scaling experiments; and downstream action recognition.

The results support the principal usefulness claim. RT-Mesh is efficient and competitive with the strongest point-cloud baseline, tensor inputs generalize better on the cross-subject and cross-action splits, performance improves consistently with training-set scale, and radar improves RGB/depth fusion in several settings.
The paper is generally clear and visually effective, and the supplementary material provides useful information on storage, data loading, actions, training, and modality-specific preprocessing.
weaknesses: The most material weakness is insufficient quantitative validation of annotation fidelity. Meshes are predictions from SOMA rather than direct measurements, synchronization uses a manually identified gesture with 12 Hz sensor sampling, and extrinsic calibration relies partly on manual correspondence. No marker-to-mesh error, calibration residual, synchronization error, failure rate, or inter-annotator verification statistic is reported. These omissions weaken the repeated claims of precise or high-fidelity ground truth, especially for fast motions.

The evaluation does not directly establish several motivating robustness claims. There are no controlled illumination, occlusion, smoke, clothing, multipath, or sensor-corruption experiments, and all data appear to come from one controlled room and one sensor configuration. Thus, the evidence supports radar HMR in this setup but not broad real-world robustness or deployment generalization.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive supplement. RT-Mesh omits important architectural values such as convolutional layouts, N1/N2, transformer depth, attention heads, and embedding sizes. Latency lacks measurement protocol details. The stated learning-rate decay of 0.1 every five epochs over 100 epochs also appears implausibly aggressive and should be verified.

The random split is described as assigning clips rather than entire sequences. If temporally adjacent clips from the same capture sequence occur across training and testing, S1 can substantially overestimate generalization. The precise split unit, temporal exclusion policy, and official split identities need to be specified. The cross-subject and cross-action results are more informative, but no cross-environment or cross-session split is available.

Some quantitative reporting is internally inconsistent: for example, P4Transformer's S1 P1 and ALL MVE values differ between the main Table 2 and supplementary Table 6. There are also incorrect or confusing method citations in Table 2. These are correctable presentation issues, but they reduce confidence in the benchmark tables.

The term “raw radar tensor” is potentially misleading because the released representation is already FFT-processed, Cartesian-mapped intensity data rather than raw ADC samples. Exact spatial bounds, voxel resolution, quantization, proprietary preprocessing, and sparsification should be documented more precisely. Likewise, calling radar “truly privacy-preserving” is too strong because radar-derived motion, body shape, and behavioral signatures can still be sensitive or identifying.

Results are reported from single runs without uncertainty, and several conclusions rest on modest differences. For example, RT-Mesh and P4Transformer are essentially tied under S1, while fusion gains vary by split. Multiple seeds or confidence intervals would help distinguish robust findings from training variation.
